{{Short description|British-American mathematician (born 1979)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
[[File:Henry Segerman.jpg|thumb|right| text-bottom |350px|Henry Segerman at the Institute for Computational and Experimental Research in Mathematics in 2019<br />Photo by Sabetta Matsumoto]]

'''Henry Segerman''' (born 1979 in [[Manchester, UK]]) is a [[Professor]] of mathematics at [[Oklahoma State University]] in [[Stillwater, Oklahoma]] who does research in three-dimensional geometry and topology, especially [[three-manifold]]s, [[triangulation (topology)|triangulations]] and [[hyperbolic geometry]].<ref>"[https://www.math.ksu.edu/research/artmathfiles/f2_hsegerman.html Mathematical dice design and Variants of the 15-puzzle and the effects of holonomy]" Kansas State University: Department of Mathematics</ref>

He was the first person to publish a book on mathematical 3D printing,<ref>''Visualizing Mathematics with 3D Printing'' Johns Hopkins University Press (2016)  {{ISBN|978-1421420356}}</ref> and is also a [[recreational mathematician]] and [[mathematical artist]] with expertise in [[virtual reality]].<ref name=ivrpa>[https://ivrpa.org/author/henryseg/ IVRPA Profile:  Henry Segerman] International Virtual Reality Professionals Association (IVRPA)</ref>  His frequent collaborators include [[Vi Hart]], [[Elisabetta Matsumoto]] and Saul Schleimer.<ref name=guardian>"[https://www.theguardian.com/science/alexs-adventures-in-numberland/2014/oct/30/pumpkin-geometry-stunning-shadow-sculptures-that-illuminate-an-ancient-mathematical-technique Pumpkin geometry: stunning shadow sculptures that illuminate an ancient mathematical technique]" by [[Alex Bellos]], [[The Guardian]], 2014-10-30</ref><ref name=bridges/><ref name=ornes>Ornes, Stephen; ''[https://openlibrary.org/books/OL27341447M/Math_Art%20Math%20Art:%20Truth,%20Beauty,%20and%20Equations Math Art: Truth, Beauty, and Equations]'' Sterling Publishing (2019), "Projections" (Section 14) {{ISBN | 978-1454930440}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Segerman received his Master of Mathematics (MS) at the [[University of Oxford]] (2001) and then his PhD at [[Stanford University]] (2007) for the dissertation "Incompressible Surfaces in Hyperbolic Punctured Torus Bundles are Strongly Detected" under [[Steven Paul Kerckhoff]].<ref>[https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=111784 Henry Segerman] at the [[Mathematics Genealogy Project]]</ref>

He was a Lecturer at the [[University of Texas at Austin]] (2007–2010) and was a Research Fellow at [[University of Melbourne]] (2010–2013). He became an [[Assistant professor|Assistant Professor]] at [[Oklahoma State University–Stillwater|Oklahoma State University]] (2013–2018), then an [[Associate professor|Associate Professor]] (2018-2025), and then a full Professor from July 2025 to the present.<ref name=bridges>[http://gallery.bridgesmathart.org/exhibitions/2021-bridges-conference/henrys Henry Segerman], [[The Bridges Organization]]: Mathematical Art Galleries</ref><ref>[https://experts.okstate.edu/henry.segerman], [[Oklahoma State University]]: Research Faculty Directory</ref>

Segerman's research lends itself to mathematics with a strong visual component.<ref name=ornes/>  This led directly to his involvement with 3D printing. In 2016 he wrote the book ''Visualizing Mathematics With 3D Printing.''<ref name=AMM>"[https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00029890.2018.1424427?journalCode=uamm20 Visualizing Mathematics With 3D Printing by Henry Segerman]" reviewed by Laura Taalman, The [[The American Mathematical Monthly|American Mathematical Monthly]], 22 Mar 2018, pp. 379-384</ref> [[Laura Taalman]] in a review said, "Segerman's book is an inside tour of mathematics with breathtaking 3D-printed scenery."<ref name=AMM/>

==3D printing==
{{Essay-like|section|date=October 2025}} 
[[File:Triple Gear.jpg|thumb|right| text-bottom |250px|Triple gear<br />by Saul Schleimer and Henry Segerman]]
[[File:Figure eight knot complement.jpg|thumb|right| text-bottom |250px| Figure eight knot complement<br />by François Guéritaud, Saul Schleimer, and Henry Segerman]]
Mathematicians used to rely on wooden or plaster models to visualize complex geometrical shapes. Nowadays, if they can be described mathematically, we can "print" them with 3D printers.<ref name=wired>"[https://www.wired.com/2016/11/cant-imagine-shapes-4-dimensions-just-print/ Can’t Imagine Shapes in 4 Dimensions? Just Print Them Out]" By Luke Whelan, ''[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]'', Nov 15, 2016</ref> Segerman uses mathematical tools including quaternions,<ref name=monkeys>"[https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/roots-of-unity/nothing-is-more-fun-than-a-hypercube-of-monkeys/ Nothing Is More Fun than a Hypercube of Monkeys]" By Evelyn Lamb, ''[[Scientific American]]'',  May 19, 2014</ref> Euclidean and non-Euclidean geometries and [[stereographic projection]] to create instructions for 3D printers.<ref name=guardian/> Sometimes the goal is to produce a work of art.<ref name=smith>"[https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/fresh-off-the-3d-printer-henry-segermans-mathematical-sculptures-2894574/ Fresh Off the 3D Printer: Henry Segerman’s Mathematical Sculptures]" By Megan Gambino, Smithsonian Magazine, March 15, 2013</ref>  Sometimes it is to shed light on four-dimensional geometry<ref name=scientist/> or some other field such as mathematical [[group theory]].  Sometimes it is both.<ref name=monkeys/>  One of his sculptures depicts a set of monkeys joined together to form a 4-dimensional hypercube.<ref name=shadows>"[https://www.nbcnews.com/science/weird-science/artist-uses-3-d-printing-create-shadows-4-d-objects-n306781 Artist Uses 3-D Printing to Create 'Shadows' of 4-D Objects]" NBC News: Weird Science, February 16, 2015,</ref>

Segerman's techniques help us visualize a four dimensional world.<ref name=plus>"[https://plus.maths.org/content/3d-printing 3D printing mathematics] by Saul Schleimer and Henry Segerman, [[Plus Magazine]], [[Millennium Mathematics Project]]</ref>  Just as the frame of a cube can cast a shadow on a flat wall, Segerman makes analogous shadows of four dimensional objects via a 3D printer.<ref name=lamb>"[https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/observations/mathematicians-at-play-3-d-puzzl/ Mathematicians at Play: 3-D Printing Enters the 4th Dimension]" By Evelyn Lamb, ''[[Scientific American]]'', October 31, 2012</ref><ref name=scientist>"[https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn26980-sculptures-cast-shadows-from-the-fourth-dimension/ Sculptures cast shadows from the fourth dimension]" By Aviva Rutkin, [[New Scientist]], 15 February 2015</ref> Segerman has also explored kinetic artwork, designing mechanisms that move in unusual or seemingly paradoxical ways.<ref name=ornes/>{{rp|128}}

==Recreational mathematics==
Segerman has appeared as a recreational mathematician<ref>''[https://www.newyorker.com/tech/annals-of-technology/the-dice-you-never-knew-you-needed The Dice You Never Knew You Needed]'' by Siobhan Roberts, [[The New Yorker]], 26 April 2016</ref> at [[Gathering 4 Gardner]] conferences<ref>[https://www.gathering4gardner.org/author/g4g-team/page/3/ Henry Segerman] Gathering4Gardner</ref> and is a frequent contributor to [[Numberphile]].<ref>[https://samenright.com/2021/08/31/a-laymans-guide-to-recreational-mathematics-videos/ A Layman’s Guide to Recreational Mathematics Videos] Sam Enright</ref>

Combining his interests in mathematics and art he is one of 24 mathematicians and artists who make up the [[Mathemalchemy]] Team.<ref>[https://mathemalchemy.org/team-24-mathematicians-artists-of-mathemalchemy/ Mathemalchemy’s Team]</ref>

In another foray into recreational mathematics Segerman founded Dice Lab with [[mathematical artist]] Robert Fathauer. Using computer search and help from fellow recreational mathematician [[Robert A. Bosch|Robert Bosch]], they created a "numerically balanced" 120-sided die in the shape of a [[disdyakis triacontahedron]]. It is the "biggest, most complex fair die possible".<ref>[https://euro-math-soc.eu/review/mathematics-various-entertaining-subjects-volume-2 The Mathematics of Various Entertaining Subjects volume 2] [[European Mathematical Society]]</ref> They concede that the die is "expensive and there’s no real use for it", but it's still theoretically interesting.<ref name=dice>''[https://www.wired.com/2016/05/mathematical-challenge-of-designing-the-worlds-most-complex-120-sided-dice/ The Mind-Boggling Challenge of Designing 120-Sided Dice]'' Wired Magazine, May 10, 2016</ref>

==Selected papers==
Segerman does research in three-dimensional geometry and topology. Papers published in this area include:
* 2020 "[https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.15801 Ray-marching Thurston geometries]", arXiv:2010.15801 [math.GT, cs.GR, math.DS], [with Coulon, Matsumoto and Trettel], October 2020
* 2010 "[https://www.researchgate.net/publication/47797436_Veering_triangulations_admit_strict_angle_structures Veering triangulations admit strict angle structures]" [with Hodgson, Rubinstein and Tillmann] [[Geometry & Topology]], November 2010, 15(4)
* 2015 "[https://msp.org/gt/2015/19-5/p05.xhtml 1-efficient triangulations and the index of a cusped hyperbolic 3-manifold]", [with Garoufalidis, Hodgson and Rubinstein], [[Geometry & Topology]] 19 (2015), pp.&nbsp;2619–2689

A second major interest, with some overlap, is mathematical visualization & art.  Papers published in this area include:
* 2014 "[https://archive.bridgesmathart.org/2014/bridges2014-143.html The Quaternion Group as a Symmetry Group]", [with Vi Hart], Proceedings of Bridges 2014: Mathematics, pp.&nbsp;143–150
* 2012 "[https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257393588_3D_Printing_for_Mathematical_Visualisation 3D printing for mathematical visualisation]", Math. Intell. 34(4) December 2012, pp.&nbsp;56–62

==Awards==
* The paper "The [[Quaternion group|Quaternion Group]] as a Symmetry Group" (with Vi Hart) was republished in The Best Writing on Mathematics 2015.<ref>''[https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691169651/the-best-writing-on-mathematics-2015 The Best Writing on Mathematics 2015]'' Edited by Mircea Pitici, Princeton University Press (2022), {{ISBN | 978-0691169651}}</ref>
* The video "[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ivHG4AOkhYA Non-Euclidean Virtual Reality Using Ray-Marching] was a winner in the 2019 We Are Mathematics Video Competition.<ref>[https://wearemathematics2019.skild.com/skild2/wearemathematics2019/loginPage.action 2019 Winners]  We Are Mathematics Video Competition!</ref>
